title: Command-Line Arguments
description: Reading command-line arguments via argc and argv, and processing them safely.
objectives: Understand the meaning of argc and argv
Safely access and process command-line arguments

content.heading: argc and argv
content.body: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) is the form of main() that receives command-line arguments. argc (argument count) is the total number of arguments, always at least 1. argv (argument vector) is an array of C strings; argv[0] is conventionally the program's own name (as invoked, which can vary by platform/shell and shouldn't be relied on for anything beyond display purposes), and argv[1] through argv[argc - 1] are the actual arguments supplied by the user. By convention (required by the C standard), argv[argc] is always a NULL pointer, marking the end of the array — useful for iterating without needing argc in some styles of code, though checking against argc directly is more common and explicit.

content.heading: Processing Arguments Safely
content.body: Since argv[i] is a char* (a string), any argument meant to be numeric must be explicitly converted, typically with atoi()/atof() (simple but silently return 0 on invalid input, with no error indication) or the more robust strtol()/strtod() (which can report exactly how much of the string was successfully parsed, letting you detect invalid input properly). Always check argc before accessing argv[1] or beyond — accessing argv[1] when the program was run with no arguments at all reads a NULL pointer, and dereferencing/printing it as a string is undefined behavior.

content.explanation: The argc check happens before argv[1] is ever accessed. strtol's endptr lets the program detect whether the entire argument was successfully consumed as a number, catching invalid input that atoi() would have silently ignored.

keyPoints: argc is the argument count (always at least 1); argv[0] is the program name, argv[1..argc-1] are the real arguments
argv[argc] is guaranteed to be NULL, marking the array's end
Numeric arguments must be explicitly converted from strings, ideally with strtol/strtod for proper error detection
Always check argc before accessing argv[1] or beyond
commonMistakes: Accessing argv[1] without first checking argc, risking a NULL pointer dereference
Using atoi() and silently treating invalid input as 0, rather than detecting the error explicitly
Assuming argv[0] is always a full, reliable path to the executable across all platforms
